label: DeepMind safety
notes: Built 2026-10-15. Blog posts and web write-ups from Google DeepMind's AI safety work, 2016 to October 2026; companion to deepmind-safety.papers.json (no item is duplicated; the Specification Gaming essay stays in the papers lane). Sources: (1) the DeepMind Safety Research Medium blog (30 stories listed in data/research/dm-roster.json and the Medium sitemap). Medium returns a Cloudflare 403 to a plain GET (also its /p/ and ?format=json forms), and the RSS feed holds only the latest 10, all of which have other copies, so no Medium URL is used. Each story is included through another full copy: its Alignment Forum cross-post where one exists (side effects, CIDs progress, scheming evaluation, consistency training, CoT monitorability, Gemini scheming tests, SAE negative results, AGI safety approach, short course, 2024 team summary); the GDM Alignment Substack copy where the AF post is only an excerpt (Human-AI complementarity, BIDPO steering, MONA blog post); or the identical deepmind.google post (Towards Robust and Verified AI = 'Identifying and eliminating bugs in learned predictive models', Learning human objectives by evaluating hypothetical behaviour, Discovering when an agent is present, Goal misgeneralisation = 'How undesired goals can arise with correct rewards'). Skipped because no readable copy exists outside Medium: Building safe AI: specification, robustness and assurance (2018; only the AF announcement is included), Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling (2018; Krakovna's AF summary is included), Understanding agent incentives with causal influence diagrams (2019), Designing agent incentives to avoid reward tampering (2019), REALab (2020; the AF draft-papers post is included), Understanding meta-trained algorithms through a Bayesian lens (2020), What mechanisms drive agent behaviour? (2021), Alignment of language agents (2021), An EPIC way to evaluate reward functions (2021), Model-free risk-sensitive RL (2021), Avoiding unsafe states in 3D environments using human feedback (2022), Your policy regulariser is secretly an adversary (2022), and one Medium comment that is not a story. The Wayback Machine was unreachable from this environment, so archived copies were not used. Substack posts that duplicate an AF cross-post or a deepmind.google post were not added again. (2) deepmind.google/blog: all 19 index pages (451 posts back to 2016) were read and the safety, alignment, frontier-safety, interpretability and closely related responsibility posts kept (38), plus one blog.google post on Gemini 4 Argon's safety; product, partnership, health and watermarking posts were left out. Every deepmind.google, blog.google, Substack, turntrout.com and wordpress.com URL returned 200 with the article text to curl -sL -A Mozilla/5.0. (3) LessWrong/Alignment Forum: GraphQL userPosts for all 75 roster accounts (2,208 posts), filtered to each person's DeepMind tenure and to safety topics and then hand-reviewed; plus LW search for DeepMind/GDM/AXRP posts. Included: team posts (summaries, agendas, hiring posts that describe agendas, mech interp progress updates, paper presentations), safety posts written by staff during their tenure (tag 'personal'), MATS/LASR projects co-written with GDM mentors (tag 'advised', scored lower), multi-lab papers with GDM authors ('multi-org'), and AXRP interviews with GDM researchers about their DeepMind work ('interview'). Alignment Newsletter issues are included from January 2021, when Rohin Shah was at DeepMind (tag 'newsletter', low score). Excluded: work done before joining or after leaving DeepMind (e.g. Risks from Learned Optimization, Ngo's 2020 posts whose affiliation is unclear, Anthropic and Apollo work by later or earlier staff), non-safety personal posts, shortforms, events, ARENA/MATS application calls, and linkposts with almost no text (two Turner linkposts are used via their full turntrout.com versions). Scores are subjective importance estimates (100 = canonical); 'why' lines were written from each post's text. Also from tenure: eleven AI-safety posts from Victoria Krakovna's blog not cross-posted to LW.

items.ab: The question of ‘value alignment’ centres upon how to ensure that AI systems are properly aligned with human values. It can be broken down into two parts. The first part is technical and focuses on how to encode values or principles in artificial agents, so that they reliably do what they ought to do. The second part is normative, and focuses on what values or principles it would be right to encode in AI. This paper focuses on the second question, paying particular attention to the fact that we live in a pluralistic world where people have a variety of different beliefs about value.…

items.why: Krakovna's report from the first AI & Society Symposium in Tokyo, on international conversations about AI impacts and safety.
items.ab: I just spent a week in Japan to speak at the inaugural symposium on AI & Society – my first conference in Asia. It was inspiring to take part in an increasingly global conversation about AI impacts, and interesting to see how the Japanese AI community thinks about these issues. Overall, Japanese researchers seemed more open to discussing controversial topics like human-level AI and consciousness than their Western counterparts. items.ab: 15 research projects on interpretability were submitted to the mechanistic interpretability Alignment Jam in January hosted with Neel Nanda. Here, we share the top projects and results. In summary: Activation patching works on singular neurons, token vector and neuron output weights can be compared, and a high mutual congruence between the two indicates a mono-semantic MLP neuron. The Automatic Circuit Identification tool (ACDC) can be used to infer a circuit for gendered pronouns, and some of these circuits can perform even better than the full model. items.t: Mech Interp Puzzle 2: Word2Vec Style Embeddings
items.why: Mech interp puzzle about word2vec-style linear structure in language model embeddings.
items.ab: Code can be found here. No prior knowledge of mech interp or language models is required to engage with this. Language model embeddings are basically a massive lookup table. The model "knows" a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens, and each one has a separate learned embedding vector. But these embeddings turn out to contain a shocking amount of structure! Notably, it's often linear structure, aka word2vec style structure. Word2Vec is a famous result (in old school language models, back in 2013!), that `man - woman == king - queen`.
